prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of aberration correction in transmission electron microscopy, which overcame the limit set by the spherical aberration of electron lenses and made imaging and spectroscopy of individual atoms in materials routine.

statement.case_for: I keep B052 as my preferred single part after the first round, but with a clearer view of what it would take to carry it. The statutory test is discovery or invention, and I read the original experiment as the one that removed a barrier everyone had accepted: Scherzer's 1936 theorem said that round electron lenses could not be corrected, and Rose's theoretical work, Haider's hexapole corrector and Urban's demonstration on real specimens in the late 1990s showed that it could. The effect was verified at once and by independent groups, the instruments are now on thousands of sites, and what they measure (atom columns, oxygen vacancies and light-element positions at interfaces, defects in oxide heterostructures and device materials) is new physical information, not only a sharper picture. The credited names are the documented originators of the TEM corrector, covering design theory, construction and first use on specimens, and the invention is close to thirty years old, so neither maturity nor reproducibility is in doubt. Nothing said in round 1 changed these facts; what the exchange changed is my estimate of how the committee will weigh them.
statement.case_against: Honestly, the case against is serious and I do not think it is only about taste. First, only a minority of the committee has ranked B052 and every member who commented describes it as an enabling instrument, so on the evidence of this exchange it cannot win a majority against B053. Second, the STEM corrector of Krivanek, Dellby and Lupini was realised in the same years and is not credited; the three-name limit means a TEM-only citation leaves out half of a shared story, and I cannot resolve that from my own recollection. Third, I am a practising microscopist, which is a reason to discount my own enthusiasm. Fourth, I said in round 1 that the prize is for the original experiment and not the more elegant later one; I must apply that test to B053 as well as to my own candidate, and on that test Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and first demonstration are original, which is why I will not oppose that prize.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the lattice clock is not incremental after combs and ion clocks, because the magic-wavelength trap with very many atoms changes stability and the systematic budget by orders of magnitude, and she asks whether microscopy is discovery or engineering.
responses.response: I concede part of this. The comb and the single-ion clock did not contain the magic-wavelength idea, and I withdraw the word incremental for Katori's contribution. My remaining reservation is narrower: the 1e-18 record and the many-body clock programme are the kind of later, more refined performance that I told the committee should not be confused with the original experiment, so the citation must be written around the lattice concept and its first realisation, as she and Eriksson propose, and the expert report must confirm priority. On your question about discovery versus engineering, I do not think the word engineering settles anything. Scherzer's theorem was a physical limit and the corrector overcame it with new electron optics, which is the same kind of act as trapping atoms at a magic wavelength.

responses.point: Eriksson says the clocks produce a new measured quantity that tests physics, while microscopy risks being judged an instrumentation advance, and he sees B029 as a weaker attribution case than I do because excluding Parkin leaves the device-relevant giant effect uncredited.
responses.response: Your distinction between a tool that yields a new measured quantity and one that yields a better image is fair, and I accept it as the sharpest form of the objection to B052. My reply is that atomic-resolution spectroscopy and quantitative imaging do yield new measured quantities (column positions to picometre precision, local bonding and composition), but I grant that the committee will see this as less direct than a test of redshift or constants. On B029 I accept your point about Parkin and the device-relevant effect, and for that reason I no longer treat it as a competitor to the lead candidates; it stays only as an alternative, with a priority question that would need an expert report before names could be fixed.

responses.point: Mehlig argues that B013 is the clean single mechanism, that Kane and Mele supply the Z2 idea Molenkamp tested, and that the committee should weigh instrumentation consistently against discovery of a phenomenon.
responses.response: I agree that consistency is what matters, and I will state my own rule openly: an instrument qualifies if it opens a class of phenomena that could not be observed before and the result is verified, which is why I treat B052 and B053 the same way. On B013 I accept that Kane and Mele cannot be dropped without splitting one idea, and I withdraw my earlier Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan triple as my preferred option. My difficulty is not the science but the attribution, because Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang motivated the HgTe experiment and are outside any three names, and the 2016 prize overlaps in theme. I would not vote against B013 on the science, but I cannot support a triple that I think the community will contest.

responses.point: Pearce moved the lattice clock to first place and asks that the Sr-lattice priority history between the Tokyo and JILA groups be verified by expert reports before the names are fixed, while noting the pending SI redefinition and the overlap with earlier prizes.
responses.response: I share your insistence on verifying who did the original work, and the same standard applies to my own candidate with the STEM corrector. On timing I do not think the pending SI redefinition should delay a prize: the performance is already confirmed independently, and the redefinition follows from the evidence. For the chair's question on the 2005 and 2012 prizes, it is not decisive for me, provided that the citation isolates the lattice concept. If the expert reports confirm Katori and Ye as the right pair, I regard B053 as defensible on the statutes and the strongest candidate on this list for a committee that wants a clean attribution, even though I still think B052 is the better fit to the word invention.

uncertainties: Whether the STEM aberration corrector (Krivanek, Dellby, Lupini) must be credited with the TEM corrector of Rose, Haider and Urban, and whether the three-name limit allows a fair citation.
Whether the committee accepts an instrumentation invention as physics, in the face of the view that a tool producing a new measured quantity is easier to defend than one producing sharper images.
Whether expert reports will confirm Katori and Ye as the right and sufficient pair for B053, given the Sr-lattice priority history across Tokyo, JILA, SYRTE, PTB and NIST.
Whether my own closeness to the field leads me to overestimate B052, since no other member has placed it first.
statement.conflict_note: I work daily with aberration-corrected microscopes at Chalmers and develop quantitative TEM methods, so I am professionally close to B052 and I ask the committee to discount my ranking of it accordingly. I have no collaboration with Rose, Urban or Haider and none with Katori, Ye or the other credited names on the shortlist. Johansson is a Chalmers colleague without a tie to B052, and Mehlig is in the neighbouring Gothenburg physics department. My disclosure is otherwise unchanged from round 1.
